issues.legal_issue: A party on remand cannot use the proceedings to return to an earlier stage or reopen matters foreclosed by an unappealed appealable remand order.
material_facts: The defendant was placed ex parte, and the plaintiff’s witnesses were examined in the defendant’s absence.
The remand order was appealable and neither party appealed it.
On remand, the defendant sought fresh evidence and to have the plaintiff’s witnesses recalled for cross-examination.
issues.conclusion: The remand order had become final and circumscribed the trial court’s jurisdiction; the defendant could not use the remand proceedings to recall the witnesses and set the proceedings back.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 105(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, an unappealed appealable remand order becomes final and its correctness cannot later be disputed; the court on remand is bound by its terms. Nainsingh v. Koonwarjee was relied on for that rule. Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal, Kotah and Arjun Singh v. Mohindra Kumar explain that a party may join proceedings at a later stage but must accept what has already occurred and cannot turn back the clock.

rule.if: proceeding_on_remand and remand_order_appealable and remand_order_not_appealed and party_seeks_to_rewind_proceedings

predicates.proceeding_on_remand: The court is conducting proceedings after a case has been remanded to it.
predicates.remand_order_appealable: The order remanding the case could be appealed.
predicates.remand_order_not_appealed: Neither party appealed the remand order.
predicates.party_seeks_to_rewind_proceedings: A party seeks to return to an earlier stage by reopening prior evidence or having witnesses recalled.

issues.definition: When a case is on remand, the remand order was appealable but unappealed, and a party seeks to rewind the proceedings, that party cannot reopen prior proceedings.

issues.legal_issue: In a suit for specific performance, equitable discretion may warrant setting aside the decrees and ordering a fresh disposal with an opportunity for both parties to adduce evidence in exceptional circumstances.
material_facts: The dispute concerned specific performance of an agreement to sell a small piece of property, described as the defendant’s only worldly goods.
The plaintiff did not enter the witness box or tender evidence.
The defendant had been unable to cross-examine the plaintiff’s witnesses because they were examined while the defendant was ex parte.
issues.conclusion: In the interests of complete justice, the Court set aside the decrees and remitted the suit for fresh disposal, allowing both parties to adduce fresh evidence and the defendant to have the witnesses recalled for cross-examination.
issues.legal_principle: The judgment identifies Sections 20 and 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and expressly states that specific performance is discretionary and equitable: the court must consider all relevant circumstances before granting it. The Court relied on those circumstances in ordering a fresh disposal; it cited no earlier case for this discretionary-relief determination.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.plaintiff_did_not_testify: The plaintiff did not enter the witness box or tender evidence.
predicates.property_is_small_and_defendants_only_wo: The suit concerns a small property that is said to be the defendant’s only worldly asset.
predicates.defendant_could_not_cross_examine_witnes: The defendant was absent when witnesses were examined and did not have the opportunity to cross-examine them.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance suit involves a plaintiff who did not testify, a small property said to be the defendant’s only worldly asset, and witnesses the defendant could not cross-examine, the court may order a fresh disposal with an opportunity for evidence.
